chapter: Columbia and the first jazz bands
title: Hearing the Original Dixieland Jazz Band; Columbia turns to Earl Fuller
summary: Kirkeby first heard New Orleans jazz via the Original Dixieland Jazz Band in 1917. Columbia, beaten by Victor, had him assemble a jazz band, so he used Earl Fuller's group and Wilbur Sweatman's small combination.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: This is an interview on the 28th of June 1961 with Ed Kirkaby, who has been a booker in New York for many years, was the originator and booker of the California Ramblers, and I find that he has some acquaintance with New Orleans items, which I believe will make his story of interest to the archives of jazz music at Tulane University. Ed, what was your first acquaintance with New Orleans music? Where did you first hear a New Orleans group, do you think?

Well, the first New Orleans group that I heard was at Risenwebers, and that was the original Dixieland Jazz Band, which came up in 1917. I was with the Columbians, I said at the time, and I believe from the records, but my memory is very vague on the thing, that they made a couple of records for Columbia at that time, which for some reason or other were not put out. Victor finally signed them up, and the reception of the public was so great that Columbia tore its hair out and got after me, and got after me, who had an assistant manager's birth there, in charge of popular records, to get a jazz band together. So it was then that I turned to Earl Fuller, who had a Richter Novelty Orchestra with some very fine New York musicians in it at the time, and Earl also, and Earl also, by the way, had the Ted Lewis in a jazz band up in the upstairs after hours room, and it was to him naturally, I turned, and he came down, and I think that Earl Fuller's jazz band was the first jazz band records that Columbia put out.

It may have been the first jazz band that was derived from the New Orleans, the original New Orleans jazz band, too, was it? Do you remember anybody else imitating the original New Orleans jazz band style?

Well, we did make some records down there with Wilbur Swetland. He had a small combination, but the style to me, again, is vague. I haven't heard of Wilbur Swetland record since I left the company, which was in 1918, but those are the two, I was called jazz bands, bands that played jazz, let's put it that way, that I recollect of the Columbia, because in those days, jazz was pretty much of an unheard proposition.
Well, I don't know that this particular experience indicates that Victor was more enterprising, at least they were more...

Commercially minded, and they saw the fact that the original Dixie Land had rising members, was a terrific sensation. People could dance to the tempo, the two-beat tempo, and the result was that their business was fabulous. So, from a commercial sales aspect, the sensible thing was to get records on the market. And when Victor beat Columbia to the punch and got them on the market, why, they did a terrific business.
